explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus says five were foolish and five were wise. Ten lamps, ten virgins, and two very different kinds of planning. I've stamped enough cookies to know the dough doesn't care how you feel about the recipe, so this split matters.

Nothing in the story says a word about money, friend. Jesus says five were foolish and five were wise (Matthew 25:2). The difference He points to is how they got ready, not what was in their pockets. So the word is wise.

Good guess, but Jesus never mentions bravery here. He says five were foolish and five were wise (Matthew 25:2). Nobody in this story fights a lion or climbs a wall, so bravery isn't what separates them. It's wise, and you'll see why very soon.

That's it, baker. The foolish ones took their lamps but did not take along any extra oil (Matthew 25:3). A lamp with no backup oil is like me showing up to a bake with the stamper and zero dough. It looks ready from far away, and that's about all it has going for it.

Cloaks never come up in this story, friend. The text says the foolish ones took their lamps but did not take along any extra oil. The missing piece wasn't something to wear, it was something to burn. So the answer is extra oil.

No staffs in this story, friend. Jesus says the foolish ones took their lamps but did not take along any extra oil (Matthew 25:3). I know a walking stick feels like the kind of thing people forget, but the text names the oil. Keep your eyes on that flask, because it comes back.

Close, but the text says something bigger. When the bridegroom was delayed, "they all became drowsy and fell asleep" (Matthew 25:5). All of them, wise and foolish alike. So being sleepy isn't what separates the two groups.

Right, friend. The text says that when the bridegroom was delayed, “they all became drowsy and fell asleep.” (Matthew 25:5) That means all ten, the wise ones too. Sleeping wasn't the difference between them, and I think that's kind of comforting.

Not quite, friend. When the cry rang out at midnight, “Then all the virgins woke up and trimmed their lamps.” (Matthew 25:7) That includes the foolish ones. They heard it just fine, and the trouble showed up right after that.

That's right. The text says, “Then all the virgins woke up and trimmed their lamps.” (Matthew 25:7) The foolish ones heard the cry like everybody else. Nobody slept through it, so the real problem is coming in the next verse.

That's what they say, baker. The foolish ones tell the wise, “Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out.” (Matthew 25:8) I'd say that's a stressful sentence to say out loud at midnight. Their lamps are the whole reason they're out there.

explanations.answer: They spilled theirs on the road
explanations.explanation: The story doesn't mention any spill, friend. The foolish ones just say, “Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out.” (Matthew 25:8) How it got that low, the text doesn't say, so I won't invent a mess for them. Their lamps going out is the reason they give.

Cracked flasks would make a dramatic story, but that's not this one. The text says the foolish ones took their lamps but did not take along any extra oil (Matthew 25:3), so there weren't flasks to crack. What they say at midnight is, “Give us some of your oil; our lamps are going out.” (Matthew 25:8)

I get why you'd hope so, friend. But the wise ones answer, “No,” and then explain that there may not be enough for both them and the foolish ones (Matthew 25:9). They don't hand over any oil. They point the foolish ones somewhere else instead.

Yes, that's what the text says. The wise ones answer, “No,” saying there may not be enough for both them and the foolish ones (Matthew 25:9). It's a tough moment, and I think it catches a lot of bakers off guard. They send the foolish five to someone else for oil.

explanations.answer: There may not be enough for both
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The wise ones say, “…or there may not be enough for both us and you.” (Matthew 25:9) That's the reason they give, and it's the only one the text gives. Five flasks only stretch so far.

explanations.answer: The bridegroom told them not to
explanations.explanation: The text never says that, friend. The bridegroom isn't even there yet when they talk. The wise ones give their own reason: “…or there may not be enough for both us and you.” (Matthew 25:9)

explanations.answer: They plan to sell it later
explanations.explanation: No selling plans in this story. The wise ones say, “…or there may not be enough for both us and you.” (Matthew 25:9) The ones who sell oil are the ones the wise tell the foolish to go to. So the reason is simply that there may not be enough.

That's right. The wise ones say, “Instead, go to those who sell oil and buy some for yourselves.” (Matthew 25:9) It's an actual plan, not a slammed door. I just think midnight is a rough hour to go shopping.

This one is actually in the text, friend. After saying no, the wise ones tell them, “Instead, go to those who sell oil and buy some for yourselves.” (Matthew 25:9) So they do point the foolish ones somewhere. They just don't give up their own oil.

Hang on, friend, because the text goes the other way. While the foolish ones were on their way to buy oil, the bridegroom arrived (Matthew 25:10). Those who were ready went in with him to the banquet. Nobody was held back for the shoppers.

Right. The text says, “But while they were on their way to buy it, the bridegroom arrived.” (Matthew 25:10) The ones who were ready went in with him, and the foolish five weren't there yet. The timing is the whole story, baker.

Yes, baker. The ones who were ready went in with the bridegroom to the wedding banquet, “and the door was shut.” (Matthew 25:10) Three small words, and a lot of weight. I think this is the moment the story turns.

I'd love an open door too, friend, but the text says otherwise. Those who were ready went in with the bridegroom, “and the door was shut.” (Matthew 25:10) That's why the foolish ones have to call out to be let in later.

No guards are mentioned anywhere in this story. The text says those who were ready went in with the bridegroom, “and the door was shut.” (Matthew 25:10) A plain shut door is all there is. And it's enough to make the next verse feel very quiet.
That's what he says. He replies, “Truly I tell you, I do not know you.” (Matthew 25:12) I think this one hurts, friend. It's the heaviest line in the whole story, so we'll let it sit for a second.

The text doesn't give them a second appointment, friend. The bridegroom replies, “Truly I tell you, I do not know you.” (Matthew 25:12) I think this is a hard line to read. It's the answer the foolish virgins get at the door.

He doesn't tell them to wait, friend. The bridegroom replies, “Truly I tell you, I do not know you.” (Matthew 25:12) I think this is one of the hardest lines in the story. That's the whole reply they get.

explanations.answer: You do not know the day or the hour
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” (Matthew 25:13) Earlier, Jesus says only the Father knows that day (Matthew 24:36). That's why my ovens stay warm and ready, baker. I'm not guessing at a date, I'm just keeping the oven on.

explanations.answer: The bridegroom always comes at midnight
explanations.explanation: In this story the cry did ring out at midnight (Matthew 25:6), but Jesus never says it's always midnight. His reason is, “…because you do not know the day or the hour.” (Matthew 25:13) That's the point. If you could set your watch by it, you wouldn't need to keep watch.

explanations.answer: The night is almost over now
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says the night is almost over, friend. He ends with, “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.” (Matthew 25:13) So the reason to keep watch isn't a countdown. It's that nobody knows the day or the hour.
